Judge Rules DHS Unlawfully Took Control of FEMA Staffing in Push for 50% Cut.

FEMA supervisors opposed the proposed reduction. The judge found that Homeland Security overrode the agency’s staffing authority and that officials deleted messages about the decisions.

A federal judge has ruled that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) unlawfully interfered with the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) authority over its workforce during a push to cut staffing by roughly half.

In an order issued September 11, 2026, U.S. District Judge Susan Illston found that DHS directed FEMA toward a staffing target of 11,383 employees for the coming fiscal year. That was roughly half of the approximately 23,000 employees used as the comparison in the court record, despite objections from FEMA supervisors and its chief human capital officer.

FEMA did not carry out the full 50% cut. The ruling addresses how the plan was developed, who controlled FEMA’s personnel decisions, and what relief may still be needed.

Where did the staffing target come from?

Senior DHS officials directed FEMA leadership in late 2025 to produce a plan projecting a sharply smaller workforce. Illston questioned the basis for the 11,383-person target, writing that it appeared to have been “pulled from thin air.”

The record showed that Karen Evans, then FEMA’s acting head, submitted the figure and then worked to justify it. FEMA supervisors and the agency’s chief human capital officer had objected to a cut of that size. Their objections left a central question unanswered: Who decided FEMA should lose half its workforce?

Disaster-response workers were a focus.

The plan affected Cadre of On-Call Response/Recovery (CORE) employees—full-time workers who help communities prepare for and recover from disasters. Their appointments typically last two to four years and have historically often been renewed.

DHS revoked FEMA’s longstanding authority to renew CORE appointments and instructed the agency in January to allow at least some appointments to expire. FEMA later moved away from broad non-renewal, but Illston found that DHS still limits CORE renewals to 180 days at a time.

The judge found no reasoned explanation in the record for revoking FEMA’s renewal authority or imposing the later conditions.

Why the judge found DHS’s actions unlawful

The Post-Katrina Emergency Management Reform Act of 2006 protects FEMA’s role within DHS. It bars the department from substantially or significantly reducing FEMA’s authorities, responsibilities, or functions.

Illston found that DHS had “unlawfully usurped” FEMA’s authority to make its own personnel decisions. The ruling concerns DHS’s control over the staffing actions in this case; it does not establish that FEMA can never change the size of its workforce.

The decision came in a broader lawsuit brought by the American Federation of Government Employees, the AFL-CIO, and other labor groups challenging federal workforce reductions.

Deleted Signal messages left a gap in the record

Illston also found that Evans and Joseph Guy, a former DHS deputy chief of staff, discussed FEMA and CORE staffing on Signal using personal phones. Their messages were set to disappear after one to four weeks.

After Evans was named a defendant in March 2026, she shortened an auto-delete timer. She created a backup in April, but the judge found that the most relevant earlier messages had already been deleted.

Illston concluded that the officials acted with the intent to deprive the plaintiffs of evidence. The court will therefore presume the lost messages would have been unfavorable to the government, providing further evidence about the staffing plan, DHS’s control and its actions. The judge also barred the government from relying on earlier testimony denying the plan or DHS’s involvement.

Illston noted that Evans had previously served as DHS chief information officer, with responsibility involving records-preservation policies. Because the messages are gone, the court may never have a complete account of how the 50% target was chosen.

Why the staffing dispute matters

An August report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that more than 4,300 employees left FEMA in fiscal year 2025. FEMA officials told investigators those departures caused a loss of experienced personnel and institutional knowledge.

GAO also found that FEMA made workforce decisions without analyzing the staff and skills needed to carry out its mission. The watchdog warned that staff reductions and a lack of planning may affect disaster readiness. It did not determine that the proposed 50% cut caused a failure in any specific disaster response.

FEMA has said it maintains experienced leadership and support staff across its headquarters and regional offices.

What happens next

Illston granted partial summary judgment to the unions on their Administrative Procedure Act claims and denied the government’s cross-motion. She did not order an immediate remedy. The unions have sought to cancel CORE non-renewal notices and reinstate affected workers.

The parties must try to agree on the scope of relief. If they cannot, they must file a joint statement identifying what remains unresolved by October 9, 2026. The court said it would then rule on relief.
